fields.connection: [topic A]。 + それはそうと、 + [topic B]
examples: The project's going well, huh. By the way, who's going on next week's business trip?
Let's stop here for today. By the way, have you seen this document?
Thanks. By the way, can you tell me how to get to the station?
The story about the new product is interesting. By the way, is the budget enough?
That movie was good. By the way, did you finish your homework?
fields.explain:
Often used in everyday conversation to steer over to another topic.
Avoid using it too abruptly with a superior in a formal context; consider ところで/さて.
Placed at the beginning of a sentence: a new sentence, right after the period of the previous one.

• Meaning: a connecting phrase for shifting the topic, often rather sudden but gentle.
• Nuance: casual, somewhat everyday; carries the feeling of “suddenly remembering something else”.
• Link: may be loosely related or unrelated to A.
fields.notes:
• Often used to slip in a “reminder” you have just remembered during a conversation.
• For a more coherent flow in a formal presentation, use さて/次に/では instead of それはそうと.
• It carries no cause-and-effect or contrast relation; it is only a signal of a topic shift. explain: Used when changing the topic. ⏐ examples: 1. 「今日の授業、おもしろかったね。」
「うん、すごくためになった。それはそうと、今度の試験いつだっけ？」
Today's class was interesting, wasn't it? Yeah, I learned a lot. By the way, when is the next exam again?
2. 「春になりましたね。それはそうと、田中さんの息子さん、大学受かったでしょうか。」
It's spring now, isn't it? By the way, I wonder if Mr. Tanaka's son got into university.
mistakes: Choosing それはそうと for a sentence that needs “cause-result” → incorrect (use だから/そのため/それで).
Using it mid-sentence or after a comma within the same long sentence → unnatural; the standard position is after the period of the previous sentence.
Confusing it with それでは (opening the next step in a presentation) → different function.

rows: Sudden topic shift, not necessarily related
<ruby>終<rt>お</rt></ruby>わり。それはそうと、<ruby>次<rt>つぎ</rt></ruby>は？
ところで、<ruby>明日<rt>あした</rt></ruby>の<ruby>件<rt>けん</rt></ruby>。
Implies “skip A to get to the main point B”
それはさておき、<ruby>本題<rt>ほんだい</rt></ruby>へ。
Very colloquial, announces a change of topic
<ruby>話<rt>はなし</rt></ruby>は<ruby>変<rt>か</rt></ruby>わるけど、さ...

fields.meaning: I really want…, if only… (earnest wish)
examples: I'd like to stay at a luxury hotel like this at least once.
I work this hard, so I really wish they'd raise my salary a little.
fields.notes: Used together with expressions of desire such as 「たい」 and 「ほしい」 to emphasize that feeling.

examples: No sooner had it rained than it cleared up.
The baby cried and then immediately burst out laughing.
The moment the store opened, a line formed in no time.
Just when I thought he'd come back, he went off somewhere again.
In this season, just when it gets cold, it suddenly turns hot.
Just as the bell rang, a power outage made everything quiet again.
fields.explain:
Point in time: used for two events that follow each other very closely.
Person: usually objective observation; avoid using the speaker's intentional action in the second clause.
Nuance: emphasizes surprise/speed; can be used to complain about erratic changes.
Style: common in spoken language, also appears in written language describing phenomena.

• Expresses that B happens almost immediately after A, giving the speaker a “flash-like”, surprising feeling.
• Usually used for objective observation (the subject is usually a third party/thing); the speaker does not intentionally intervene.
• The second clause is usually a surprising fact/phenomenon; not suitable for commands, intentions, or direct invitations.
• Can express repeated, opposite changes: A, then immediately the opposite B.
• Emotional nuance: surprise, annoyance, mild complaint, or describing a fast pace of change.
fields.notes:
• The second clause uses a factual/objective form (～た／～ている／～たところだ...). Avoid ～ましょう、～てください.
• Often used with natural phenomena, other people's behavior, and changes of state.
• For repeated opposite changes, the pattern helps describe a “sunny in the morning, rainy in the afternoon” character.
mistakes: Using a command/volition in the second clause: 読んだかと思ったら、勉強しよう× → Use a fact/observation.
Using it for the speaker's own intentional action: 私は家に着いたかと思ったら、寝ます× → Unnatural.
Confusing it with ～と思いきや (contrary to expectation) or ～たとたん (an unintended incident). Read the nuance of the question carefully.
The time between the two clauses must be very short; if it is long, use ～てから or ～その後.

rows: ～たかと<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>ったら/～たかと<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>うと
Emphasizes surprise; second clause is not a command/intention
<ruby>帰<rt>かえ</rt></ruby>ったかと<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>うと、また<ruby>出<rt>で</rt></ruby>た。
B is usually an unintended incident; the subjects of both clauses are usually the same
<ruby>立<rt>た</rt></ruby>ち<ruby>上<rt>あ</rt></ruby>がったとたん、<ruby>倒<rt>たお</rt></ruby>れた。
Expresses an even closer degree; more neutral nuance
<ruby>終<rt>お</rt></ruby>わるか<ruby>終<rt>お</rt></ruby>わらないかのうちに<ruby>帰<rt>かえ</rt></ruby>る。
As soon as A, immediately B
Formal/old written style; not used with commands
<ruby>着<rt>つ</rt></ruby>くや<ruby>否<rt>いな</rt></ruby>や、<ruby>会議<rt>かいぎ</rt></ruby>が<ruby>始<rt>はじ</rt></ruby>まった。
I thought A, but unexpectedly B
Not necessarily “immediate”; emphasizes contrary to expectation
<ruby>簡単<rt>かんたん</rt></ruby>かと<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>いきや、<ruby>難<rt>むずか</rt></ruby>しい。

examples: He left home last year and hasn't come back even once since.
I met that person only once, and I haven't been in touch with them since.
I bought this book and just left it on the shelf without reading it.
I got a phone call, and after that I haven't heard a thing.
Since his illness, my grandfather has been almost entirely bedridden.
She graduated, and since then I haven't seen her around town.
fields.explain:
Often used with personal events as a reference point (contact, returning, meeting, studying...).
Nuance: slightly negative/regretful, or the objective sense “from then on, that was it”.
Time: lasts up to the observed present; equivalent to “ever since A, still...”.

• “Since A, (the expected thing) has not happened again” → emphasizes a prolonged interruption.
• Usually accompanied by a negative (～ない／～ていない) in the second clause. Without a negative, the nuance is still “only that once” → less natural in this meaning.
• Focuses on the “only, once” nature of a past action and its consequences lasting until now.
• Often used in spoken language describing the state of contact, meeting, returning, and changes.
fields.notes:
• In conversation, っきり is more common than きり after a verb.
• 寝たきり is a fixed phrase meaning “bedridden”, used descriptively in a medical/social sense.
• In written language you may see ～たきりだ／～たきりで (subject-predicate shortened) to emphasize a lasting state.
mistakes: Dropping ない in the second clause distorts the main meaning: 連絡したきり。× → 連絡したきり（連絡が）来ない。/ 連絡していない。
Confusing it with ～て以来: if there is an implication of “should have... but didn't”, prefer ～たきり.
Using it for naturally repeating events (the sun rising/setting) is unnatural.
Confusing it with ～っきり meaning “only”: 会ったっきり＝会って以来（not met again), which is different from 一回だけ会った.

rows: Emphasizes the interruption and the expectation that it should have happened again
<ruby>会<rt>あ</rt></ruby>ったきり、<ruby>連絡<rt>れんらく</rt></ruby>しない。
More neutral, just a point in time; no expectation necessarily
<ruby>卒業<rt>そつぎょう</rt></ruby>して<ruby>以来<rt>いらい</rt></ruby>、<ruby>東京<rt>とうきょう</rt></ruby>にいる。
Emphasizes a big change, more formal
<ruby>子<rt>こ</rt></ruby>が<ruby>生<rt>う</rt></ruby>まれてからというもの、<ruby>外食<rt>がいしょく</rt></ruby>しない。
Different meaning; just leaving/neglecting things as they are
<ruby>電気<rt>でんき</rt></ruby>をつけっぱなし。
Does not mean “ever since”; do not confuse with っきり (only)

fields.meaning: Although…, still…; even though (I) know…, still…
fields.connection: Vます(drop ます) + つつも
examples: Although I had half given up, thinking I wouldn't make it in time, I ran desperately.
Although I mean to study, I keep thinking about my girlfriend and can't.
Although my leg is gradually getting better, it will take another half a year before I can run.
fields.notes:
meaning_vi: (1) Although …
(2) While/at the same time … ⏐ explain: (1) Often used when the speaker confesses, regrets, reconsiders… ⏐ examples: 1. 彼女は忙しいと言いつつ、長電話をしている。
She says she's busy, yet she's chatting away on the phone.
2. 今日こそがんばろうと思いつつ、また勉強しなかった。
Although I thought I'd really work hard starting today, I didn't study again.
3. 先生と相談しつつ、進路を決めたいと思う。
I want to decide my future path while consulting with my teacher.

fields.meaning: Cannot keep on…, cannot just go on…
examples: I can't just keep waiting for the results, so I'll inquire directly.
I can't stay down forever. Let's move forward.
I can't take it easy. The deadline is close.
You can't just keep crying, you know.
We can't dawdle here. Let's evacuate quickly.
fields.explain:
Often used with stative verbs: 待つ／落ち込む／のんびりする／迷っている…
Nuance of urgency, determinedly pushing yourself; mostly spoken language, but fine in ordinary written language too.
Polite negative form: ～いられません. The contracted forms sound stronger: ～てられない／～ちゃいられない.

• Expresses a situation where you cannot continue a state/action any longer because of time pressure, responsibility, or circumstances.
• Implies the speaker realizes they must change their action right away: “I can't just keep … forever”.
• Unlike “cannot in terms of ability” (できない), this pattern means “cannot because of the situation/urgency”.
fields.notes:
• Often accompanied by a reason/circumstance right after or before the sentence: 締め切りがあるから、待っていられない。
• Emphasizes switching actions: the following sentence is often an alternative (直接問い合わせる／行動に移す…).
• The てられない form is common in conversation, stressing urgency.
meaning_vi: Cannot keep on … forever
explain: Nuance of determination: acknowledging the current situation but emphasizing “things must change”.
Often appears with a pressing reason/circumstance: 時間がない／責任がある／状況が厳しい…
Suitable for both spoken and written language; in speeches/meetings it shows a spirit of change.
examples: 1. 締め切りが近いから、遊んでばかりはいられない。
The deadline is close, so I can't just keep playing.
2. 失敗したけど、いつまでも泣いてばかりはいられない。
I failed, but I can't keep crying forever.
3. もう社会人だ。親に甘えてばかりはいられない。
I'm a working adult now. I can't keep depending on my parents.
4. いつまでも学生でばかりはいられない。自立しなければ。
I can't stay a student forever. I have to become independent.
5. 危機の今、守りに回ってばかりはいられない。
Now, in a crisis, we can't just stay on the defensive.
6. わからないからといって、人に聞いてばかりはいられない。
Just because you don't understand, you can't keep asking other people all the time.
comparison: Pattern | Meaning | Difference | Short example
Vてばかりはいられない | Cannot keep doing V forever | Emphasizes changing actions | 寝（ね）てばかりはいられない
N/なでばかりはいられない | Cannot stay in state N/な forever | Uses “で” to connect N/Aな | 学生（がくせい）でばかりはいられない
～てばかりだ | Doing nothing but V | Describes the current situation, no implication of needing to change | 遊（あそ）んでばかりだ
～てはいられない | Cannot keep V-ing | Without “ばかり” → emphasizes being unable to continue the behavior | 悠長（ゆうちょう）にしてはいられない
～ばかりではない | Not only… | Negates “only”; different meaning | 彼（かれ）は遊（あそ）びばかりではない
common_mistakes: • Wrong form with N/Aな: ×学生ばかりはいられない → 学生でばかりはいられない.
• Using the dictionary form: ×遊ぶばかりはいられない → 遊んでばかりはいられない.
• Confusing it with ～てばかりだ (describing a habit) → it lacks the nuance of “must change”.
• JLPT N2: a trap distinguishing ～てはいられない and ～てばかりはいられない; note the core meaning “cannot just do one thing”.
meaning_vi: Cannot keep on…, have no time to… (てはいられない)
meaning_vi: Cannot keep on… forever (てばかりはいられない)
meaning_vi: Cannot continue …, cannot keep on …
examples: 1. 田中君、遅いなあ。もう待ってられないから先に行こう。
Tanaka's so late. We can't wait any longer, so let's go on ahead.
2. 忙しくてテレビなんか見てらんない。
I'm so busy I can't sit around watching TV.
meaning_vi: Cannot keep … forever
examples: 1. 連休だけれど、もうすぐ試験があるから、遊んでばかりはいられない。
It's a long holiday, but I have an exam soon, so I can't just play.
2. もう親に頼ってばかりはいられない。
I can't keep relying on my parents anymore.
mistakes: Confusing “cannot in terms of ability” with “cannot because of the situation”: ×疲れて走っていられない（may be correct if it means “cannot keep running” because of tiredness; do not confuse it with 走れない）.
Leaving out the reason makes the sentence sound abrupt: state the circumstance/urgency to sound more natural.
Wrong subject: the pattern usually expresses the speaker's own feeling; avoid imposing it on a third party unless it is a clear conjecture.

rows: Full form; same meaning as Vていられない
Vている<ruby>場合<rt>ばあい</rt></ruby>じゃない
This is no time to V
<ruby>遊<rt>あそ</rt></ruby>んでいる<ruby>場合<rt>ばあい</rt></ruby>じゃない
Moral/social reason, not because of being busy
<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>かないわけにはいかない
Strongly expressive, does not mean “cannot continue”

fields.connection: Vて + はかなわない / V passive form て + はかなわない (来られてはかなわない)
examples: The customer simply made a mistake on their own, so I can't stand being blamed for it.
It's too much having people come over to hang out every time I have a day off.

fields.meaning: Is it…?, could you call it…?
fields.connection: V/A plain form + というのか / N/Na(だ) + というのか
examples: I still don't know whether this is what you call love or just admiration.
Whether you call his attitude rude or insensitive, anyway, it makes me angry.
After all that effort, is this what the result is?
I don't know whether to call it happiness or anxiety; it's a complicated feeling.
Whether you call this a miracle or a coincidence, anyway, it's unbelievable.
fields.explain:
Usually at the end of the sentence or mid-sentence, expressing inner thoughts or hesitant feelings that are hard to put into words.
Used in spoken language or in written language describing emotions, not in formal written language such as reports or theses.
The intonation is usually that of a light question or exclamation, but it is not a question that requires an answer.

• Expresses hesitation when you want to name, evaluate or express something: “Can you say it is…?”, “What should I call it?”.
• Often contains emotions such as surprise, irony, disbelief, or difficulty expressing oneself.
• Can be used to make a gentle judgment or express doubt: “Is it right to call it…?”.
• Often used in conversation or in writing that describes a character's inner state.
fields.notes:
• This pattern is often used to describe a state of indecision in literature, anime, and movies.
• It can be repeated twice to present two options: ～というのか、～というのか.
• Unlike an ordinary question, this is a rhetorical question that does not need an answer from the listener.
mistakes: Confusing it with というのに/ということだ → look at the nuance: an exclamatory question or a paradox.
Using it in a formal context: this pattern is emotional and not used in academic texts.
Missing the first clause/second clause: information to compare is needed; otherwise the sentence will be vague.

rows: Hesitation, hard to express, complicated feelings.
<ruby>才能<rt>さいのう</rt></ruby>というのか、<ruby>運<rt>うん</rt></ruby>というのか。
<ruby>民主<rt>みんしゅ</rt></ruby><ruby>主義<rt>しゅぎ</rt></ruby>というのは…
<ruby>雨<rt>あめ</rt></ruby>だというのに<ruby>出<rt>で</rt></ruby>かけた。
<ruby>彼<rt>かれ</rt></ruby>は<ruby>怒<rt>おこ</rt></ruby>っているのではないか。

examples: Even though it's this cold, he isn't even wearing a coat.
I want them to come home soon, and yet I haven't even heard from them.
Even though it was pouring, the game wasn't canceled.
Even though the pay is low, I'm constantly made to work overtime.
Even though she was busy, she helped me.
fields.explain:
Position: between two clauses A and B. A is a fact, B is an opposite, unwanted result.
Usually carries negative emotions: reproach, disappointment, complaint.
Can be used in spoken language, but has a strong nuance → use it when you want to emphasize something unreasonable.
Not suitable for scientific writing or overly formal situations such as political speeches.

• A sentence pattern expressing a strong contrast between reality and expectation: although A is a fact, the result is B, which is surprising, frustrating or blameworthy.
• Strong emotional nuance: expresses anger, complaint, disappointment, even sarcasm.
• Natural translations: “Even though… still…”, “And yet…”, “Despite… nevertheless…”.
• Differs from (ordinary) 〜のに in that というのに is stronger emotionally and is used a lot in written language and expressive conversation.
fields.notes:
• Often used in novels and emotionally charged dialogue such as in movies, anime, and essays.
• The polite form 「というのです／というのにです」 is rarely used; the plain form is usual.
• Be careful to distinguish its pronunciation from 「というのに？」 (asking back: “you mean…, right?”).
mistakes: Confusing it with ～というのに？ (question) → the question uses intonation, while the grammar point expresses contrast.
Confusing it with ～のに: remember that というのに is stronger and emotional.
Using it in the wrong context when the sentence contains no emotion or no clear contrast.
The JLPT N2 often tests the difference from ～にもかかわらず and ～のに.

rows: Strong emotion, indignation, contrary to expectation.
<ruby>雨<rt>あめ</rt></ruby>というのに<ruby>出<rt>で</rt></ruby>かけた。
Formal, more common in written language.
<ruby>雨<rt>あめ</rt></ruby>にもかかわらず<ruby>試合<rt>しあい</rt></ruby>が<ruby>行<rt>おこな</rt></ruby>われた。
<ruby>知<rt>し</rt></ruby>っているくせに<ruby>教<rt>おし</rt></ruby>えてくれない。

fields.connection: [sentence A]。というのも、[sentence B](からだ)
examples: I don't talk with him much. That's because our personalities don't match.
I'll be busy next week. The reason is that a new project is starting.
I can't go out today. That's because the rain is terrible.
The game was canceled. That's because a typhoon is approaching.
He quit his company. That's because he plans to open his own shop.
fields.explain:
Placed at the beginning of clause b to explain clause a.
More formal than だって or なんでかというと.
Often used when explaining in polite conversation, newspapers, essays, and argumentative writing.
It differs from というのは in that というのは introduces a reason, while というのも emphasizes “this is the reason for what was just said”.

• Used to give a reason or explanation for the preceding clause.
• Equivalent to “The reason… is that…”, “The reason is…”.
• Clause A is a conclusion or fact. Clause B (after というのも) is the cause or reason.
• Often used in written language and formal spoken language, especially in argumentative, explanatory, or persuasive writing.
fields.notes:
• よく used in essays and argumentative writing, when you want to present things coherently.
• Can be combined with the polite form: ～ということです・～というのです.
• If the reason is long, it can be inverted: というのも、～からだ。
mistakes: Confusing it with ということだ (hearsay / conclusion) – a completely different function.
Not used in simple casual speech – it sounds stiff; use だって/なんでかというと.
What follows というのも must be a reasonable reason; do not use it for unrelated information.
The JLPT N2~N1 often asks you to distinguish it from というのは/なぜかというと.

rows: Explains the cause of the previous sentence; written language, formal.
<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>かない。というのも、<ruby>忙<rt>いそが</rt></ruby>しいからだ。
Introduces a reason or defines a word/concept.
<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>かない。というのは、<ruby>忙<rt>いそが</rt></ruby>しいからだ。
Emphasizes the reason part, often used with ～からだ.
<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>かない。なぜかというと、<ruby>忙<rt>いそが</rt></ruby>しいからだ。
<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>かないよ。だって<ruby>忙<rt>いそが</rt></ruby>しいもん。
